We use present perfect to talk about things that happened in the past and ended in the present.

You can use present perfect to express ideas in any of the three following ways:

1. Ideas where time is not important

Sometimes you use present perfect to talk about the ideas in which you express lack of time, lack of importance of time for something, or ideas about something unfinished.

As time is not important for the action, you do not mention it in any of the ideas.

Example:

Code lines have been important to edit software.
The IT personnel have fixed the software.

2. Repeated ideas

Every time actions are done repeatedly in the past but are somehow related to the present, you express them with present perfect.

Example:

I've edited the code lines several times!
We've added different code lines every time we try to fix the problem.

3. Long unfinished actions.

If you started an action in the past and is still in progress, you can use present perfect to express such idea.

Example:

The IT has struggled with that code since he got in charge of modifying the program.

In order to make a sentence in present perfect you have to use the following structure:

Subject + have/has + past participle verb + complement.

Note: you can contract the Auxiliary verb have/ has as follows:
I've been really busy with the other assignments and I really need some help.
I've tried to make this program run during the whole day.
I've worked with these codes so many times that I completely forgot to check that.

When you are working with databases, it is common to talk about CRUD procedures as it is said that if the program does not have the whole four components (create, retrieve, update and delete) the software is not complete; therefore, it won’t work.

Each procedure has to be edited and created using code lines. CRUD procedures can be created in specialized software and apps that can be either free or privative such as MySQL or Oracle among many others.

Each of the letters of CRUD represents one specific procedure:

The Create procedures allow the user to insert data into a software that can be either installed in a PC or online regarding to any topic. It can be either a name, an address or email, among many others.

The Read procedures allow the user to select or read the cells containing the information previously added.

The Update procedures allow the users to modify the data previously added in the C procedures.

The Delete procedures allow the users to delete rows of information any time the user considers this necessary.

Ronald: Hi, Paula. I was wondering if you could actually help me with a little issue I have with this database I’m generating.
Paula: Sure, what’s the deal?
Ronald: Well, I need to finish programing this database by tomorrow’s class with Mr. Fredricksen, but I’ve been really busy with the other assignments and I really need some help.
Paula: Hmm, I suppose you want me to program that for you, don’t you?
Ronald: Not really, I’d rather you help me with a fresh pair of eyes. As you can see, I’ve tried to make this program run during the whole day, but there’s no use, it used to work at the beginning but now it’s a total drag.

Paula: Let me take a glance over the codes... Ok, now I see, do you remember what CRUD stands for?

Ronald: Sure, Create, Retrieve, Update and Delete. Why do you ask?

Paula: Do you remember what they are for?

Ronald: Sure, they are by far the most important things to keep in mind when programming databases, as they permit programs to work well by allowing users to add, modify, import and delete data, as for example, a cell in a spreadsheet, but I wouldn’t worry about that, that’s something I master.

Paula: But, that’s something I’d rather you checked twice. Would you mind looking at the codes and telling me what’s missing?
Ronald: Oh my… It seems to be I forgot to add the R line while editing the codes. I’ve worked with these codes so many times that I completely forgot to check that; it’s probably because I used to work with an old template that has that error.
Paula: Well, I suppose you’ve done it wrong all this time.
Ronald: I think I’d rather check the other projects.
